newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portuguese pilots ground international flights.
newsitem.headline: Portuguese pilots ground international flights.

text.p: Pilots at state carrier TAP-Air Portugal began a 48-hour strike on Thursday ignoring government and company warnings that they were putting the loss-making airline's future at risk.

A last ditch bid to break a deadlock over working hours failed on Wednesday night and the Union of Civil Aviation Pilots (SPAC), representing the company's 430 pilots, went ahead with the threatened stoppage which mainly hit international flights.
A company spokesman said that by early morning, 11 international connections had been cancelled leaving anxious passengers with the difficult task of finding a seat on another airline.
Private carrier Portugalia handles most domestic flights, while the law obliges TAP pilots to maintain a limited service between the mainland and Portugal's Atlantic Azores and Madeira islands.
TAP, which says the strike is illegal, was offering no refunds for grounded flights.
A group of French school children, whose flight from the northern city of Oporto was cancelled, was put aboard a coach for a 25-hour drive back to Paris.
The airline, which the Socialist government wants to privatise next year, is seeking greater flexibility in working hours in an attempt to boost efficiency and cut costs.
Pilots say that they already work more than colleagues with rival European airlines and that increasing their workload threatened the safety of planes.

"TAP is not competitive. A company that is not competitive in Europe where state subsidies are no longer allowed is condemned to disappear," company chairman Manuel Ferreira Lima told journalists after the failure of Wednesday's talks.
"I am sorry to put it so starkly but the time has come for things to be understood clearly," he said.
TAP lost 10.5 billion escudos ($61 million) in 1996 but had hoped to make a profit for the first time in 23 years in 1997 in preparation for its proposed privatisation next year.
However, the company says that a two-day stoppage will cost some $6.0 million and wipe out all the expected gain.
The strike also poses the first serious labour challenge to the Socialist government of Prime Minister Antonio Guterres since it took power 18 months ago.
But in its initial reaction, the government appeared to be siding firmly with the company.
"The strike is going to bring severe lossess to the company...this way, TAP is not going to be viable," said Planning Minister Joao Cravinho whose ministry covers the aviation industry.
"TAP cannot operate in conditions that are burdensome compared with other European companies," he added.
The company, one of the few European airlines not to form part of an international alliance, has been holding talks with various potential partners.
But it says there is no chance of a deal until the issue of working hours is resolved. ($ = 172 Portugese Escudos)
